findings.text: The AP Single Window Portal is not truly “single”: departments such as the electrical department sit outside it, so applicants still have to approach each department separately.

The portal's 20 MB upload limit is too small for a full drawing set (4–5 drawings such as layout and elevations) and structural designs; some industries need 50–100 MB and have to keep requesting an increase.

Applicants find it hard to manage the process on their own and mostly rely on consultants end to end (form filling, submission, query responses, liaisoning), particularly small industries without in-house knowledge; AutoCAD drawings are effectively essential.

The building stability study must be obtained at the applicant's own cost from a government-approved/empaneled structural or civil engineer; the fee varies by engineer and industry size, and preparing the study takes considerable time.
Category-wise technical specifications and mandatory requirements are not clearly communicated to all applicants.

Requirements differ by sector and size: small units (10–15 workers) have few mandatory facilities, whereas pharma, chemical, plastics, recycling, food and red-category metal/steel manufacturing face additional mandatory requirements.

Participants describe no distinct renewal certificate system: the licence carries forward January–December once the fee is paid by 30 December, and only an acknowledgement is issued, not a fresh licence or certificate.
The fee is calculated online on horsepower/kVA, labour and workforce, and paid online directly to the government; participants did not ask for any fee reduction.
Inspection is not annual; it is triggered by incidents or changes and is risk/safety based, with the pollution category (green/yellow/red) treated as a separate PCB matter.

Applications go online through scrutiny (queries raised on the portal and by phone), an inspection about one week after submission on average, further scrutiny, and final approval, but applicants cannot see this internal sequence.
The portal shows only “pending” or “pending upload”, with no approval timeline published; approval becomes visible only at the end, when the certificate is printed.

No duplicate or redundant documents were specifically reported; drawings uploaded once are retained on the portal and auto-generated at renewal, re-uploaded only when the structure or construction plan is modified.
Timelines vary with firm size and sector (larger firms take longer), and applications are processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

Time is lost before submission in preparing documents, mainly the stability study and drawings; most participants reported no delay in scrutiny or inspection, though one recalled a case of about 6 months (details unclear in the transcript).
Participants called real-time, stage-wise application tracking with timelines, modelled on the AP incentive portal, the most important improvement.
Raise the portal upload limit above 20 MB (50–100 MB was mentioned).
Publish an FAQ and a guidance document on the portal listing mandatory documents and technical specifications by industry category, along with safety guidelines.
Participants preferred improving service quality (rather than reducing fees) and investing in skill development and skill mapping, as skilled workers are lacking.
No unrecorded or informal costs were reported; every cost in the process can be recorded in the books.
DIC is seen as the umbrella department guiding the portal; one participant reported good support at the department, though most still rely on agents.
Participants felt the gap between government intent and ground-level implementation is wide.

findings.text: Building Plan Approval requires coordinating five separate approvals/permissions (BPA/CRDA, factory licence, pollution control, fire, and DIC/Industries registration), and the coordination burden falls entirely on the applicant.

Licensed/empanelled architects are reported to be very limited in number; participants said several gave misleading guidance, which one participant linked to roughly six months of delay and added cost on a prior project.
Preparing technical documentation (e.g., drawings at a fixed 1:100 scale, specific PDF/AutoCAD formats) was described as impossible to do without a consultant, “even for techies.”
Officers reportedly raise clarification queries just before a statutory deadline expires, resetting the processing clock without materially shortening real approval time.

A land-use conversion request was first permitted only for the constructed portion of a plot (1.55 of 1.65 acres) and then rejected because the department required conversion of the entire holding, forcing re-filing.
A permit fee was reportedly filed under the wrong government “head” by the processing office, with no mechanism described to recover or reallocate the amount.

Even though a single-window portal exists, actual approvals still require dealing with each department separately on different portals (fire, pollution control board, single window, etc.), and applicants find it hard to know where their application stands.

Pollution Control Board renewal fees (cited at roughly ₹40,000 per year, with inconsistent references to monthly figures) were felt disproportionate for a self-described “green category”, zero-waste, electricity-only unit.

Property tax on a leased industrial plot was cited at roughly ₹4.7–4.8 lakh per year with no clear basis provided by the authority; an RTI filed on 20 June had not received the statutorily due reply by 20 July.

CRDA/construction-permission cost was cited at around ₹27 lakh for one project plus an additional ~14% taxation on project cost, with no clarity on how the calculation or exemption category is determined.
Deemed approval is applicable in principle, and an inspection-based (“reality check”) approval route also exists, but neither was described as consistently or transparently applied.
Applicants must register/apply separately across multiple departmental systems even though the single-window portal was intended to consolidate this.
A minor mismatch in firm-name formatting between GST registration and other portals was reported to cause complications across systems.

No dedicated single point of contact/case officer exists to coordinate one application across departments, and there is no help-desk or call-centre with a defined turnaround time for resolving department queries.

The same supporting documents for a building-plan application are reportedly resubmitted in different formats/ratios at different steps, and applicants or consultants often must visit departments in person to check status, duplicating the digital application with manual follow-up.
Shortage of, and inconsistent quality among, licensed/empanelled architects and consultants qualified to prepare and file BPA documentation contributes to delay.
Land-use conversion and construction-permission processing was cited as taking roughly one to two years in some cases.
Integrate departmental portals so application status is visible in one place, and assign a single coordinating officer per application to liaise across departments on the applicant's behalf.

Set up a help-desk/call-centre with a defined response window (participants suggested 3–5 days) for department queries, and establish a panel of government-registered/trained consultants with regulated, published, industry-specific fees.

Automate fee and category calculation from backend data to reduce manual discretion, publish sector-specific FAQs, and create a defined mechanism to recover or reallocate fees paid against an incorrect government head.

Introduce and enforce internal timelines and officer-level accountability for approvals, including a penalty framework participants understood to be under consideration (cited as a 10% deduction from application fee for delay).

Participants agreed that corruption at the ground/implementation level remains an issue to be addressed alongside procedural reform; more than one summarised the experience as “applying is easy, approval is difficult.”

findings.text: (Session 1, Visakhapatnam) Applicants lack adequate real-time visibility of their CTE application status, as updates are not consistently provided on the stage, pending status, or required action, often requiring them to contact the department directly.

(Session 1) Stakeholders are not fully clear about the applicable approval timeline for CTE, even though prescribed timelines exist, and there is no clear understanding of what happens after the prescribed timeline expires.

(Session 1) The single-window portal may redirect applicants to separate departmental websites/portals when another approval is required, creating additional logins, steps and follow-up, and sometimes requiring separate payments.
(Session 1) Applicants face uncertainty about document specifications such as file type, file size and dimensions; standardised templates and clearer upload instructions were suggested.

(Session 1) Prescribed timelines are not always reflected or monitored clearly on the portal; delayed approvals create financial pressure because investments and financing arrangements may already be in place.

(Session 1) Introduce real-time application tracking, display prescribed timelines clearly, automatically flag applications that have crossed the due date, and define a clear deemed-approval mechanism wherever applicable.

(Session 1) The call-centre facility, specifically described as the 'Ahmedabad call centre', was viewed positively for username/password and pending-application support, with good working hours and an automatic callback facility when the line is busy.
(Session 2, Nellore) Single window exists only on the portal and not in practice; applicants still have to go to the offices.
(Session 2) Policy changes are applied retrospectively to applications already submitted, leaving files in limbo while land, equipment, lease and bank-loan commitments have already been made.
(Session 2) Environmental clearance (especially for mining) takes a very long time (6 months to 1 year quoted); participants said it moves only with political influence or backing.
(Session 2) Consultants help only with filling the application; after that there is no liaisoning, so entrepreneurs chase departments themselves and files stall because the next step is unknown.
(Session 2) Records are not yet digitised, so the process cannot run fully online; applicants must meet the concerned department officer in person after queries are raised.
(Session 2) Industry is not consulted before policies are made; the single window is on paper only, and the policy intent of a single point of clearance is not being met in practice.

(Session 2) A participant indicated that about 90% of the information needed across land allotment, building plan and occupancy approvals is the same, with only 5–10% different, citing poor coordination between departments.
(Session 2) Waits of about 8–10 months before being ready to construct or start were mentioned, alongside 6-month-to-1-year environmental clearance timelines for mining-related approvals.
(Session 2) Apply the policy and rules in force on the date of submission until the government grants approval (no retrospective application), and consult industry before framing policies.
(Session 2) Provide one dedicated resource person/help desk (from DIC) to guide entrepreneurs at each step, run on all 7 days; participants said they would pay the government a fee for this.
(Session 2) Moderator noted that in some cases AP has dispensed with CFE(CTE) and a single CFO(CTO) now covers both (stated around 2025).
(Session 2) This is the second Cost of Regulation round: 13 services were covered in 2023 and 26 services in 2026.

findings.text: (Session 1, Anakapalli) No template or format exists for the Environment Management Plan (EMP); industries have the data but not the format, so they go to a consultant.

(Session 1) CTE and CTO are separate steps, so moving from CTE to CTO means another full application and inspection; for every new product the whole cycle repeats with fees and inspection, hitting pharma and fast-changing industries hardest.
(Session 1) Effluent limits are set by project size (10 KL per acre), not by industry or production, and are not enough for some products.

(Session 1) Where environmental clearance applies (scheduled activities, or construction above 20,000 sq m), a recognised consultant is mandatory; equipment requirements (e.g., online monitoring for boilers above a set limit, linked to APPCB) are shown at CTE application stage.

(Session 1) CTO is applied for online on the single desk portal as a one-time consent; after submission the application goes automatically to the PCB and other departments (e.g., fire), with inspection within about one week.
(Session 1) Documents from earlier approvals carry over on the portal, but have to be submitted again moving from CTE to CTO, and all documents have to be uploaded again at CTO renewal.
(Session 1) No delay was reported; participants said inspection time and queries after inspection were not a problem.
(Session 1) APPCB should give an EMP template or framework so no consultant is needed, and effluent limits should be set by industry and production rather than a flat per-acre figure.
(Session 1) Combine CTE and CTO into one step, and for a new product, do not repeat the full process if the pollution load stays within the approved limit, as under MoEF rules.

(Session 1) The fee is based on project cost (about 0.009%) and water/air use, for a validity of 1, 2, 5 or 7 years chosen by the industry; participants said fees are clear and on the website, and some units with in-house teams manage without a consultant.

(Session 2, Nellore) Plan-approval and CTO fees (worked out on project cost/construction area) are high and are charged even on government-allotted land and in MSME parks; consultant fees of about ₹30,000 come on top.

(Session 2) Entrepreneurs pay for utilities themselves: about ₹10.5 lakh for a power transformer even inside government-approved (APIIC) lands; another quotation of about ₹6.5 lakh was also mentioned.
(Session 2) Little information on how to apply for CTO or which documents are needed, so most units depend on consultants; no guidance exists on the next step when an entrepreneur is stuck.
(Session 2) No single responsible officer or contact point exists in each industrial park, and subsidies, including the power subsidy, take long to be released with no definite timeline.

(Session 2) Fees for approval of building/layout plans are charged on government-allotted land and in MSME parks; participants want them removed, and water/power are not provided by government in government-approved industrial lands.

(Session 2) CTO needs multiple approvals, and applicants (and consultants) are unclear which authority approves what; approval timelines differ by pollution category (white/green/orange/red) and are not clear to applicants.

(Session 2) At land registration (about one year after start), documents the unit already holds (Fire NOC, industries and labour certificates, pollution board certificate, plus a year of GST returns, accounts and bank statements) have to be submitted again.
(Session 2) Remove plan-approval fees on government-allotted land and in MSME parks, and have government provide water and power infrastructure in its industrial areas.

(Session 2) Hold district-wise orientation workshops for new entrepreneurs on the approving authority, documents required and timelines, and make one officer accountable per area/park as a single point of contact.

findings.text: (Session 1, Anakapalli) The Fire NOC now has a short validity (about 2 years in the cases discussed) and may be cut further for fresh applications; it used to be 3–5 years, and repeated renewal even when nothing has changed adds to the burden.

(Session 1) Water sprinklers do not suit sensitive areas, such as reactors and clean (aseptic) areas in pharma and food units, as water can spoil the material or process; modular fire extinguishers are treated only as an exemption, not a regular option.
(Session 1) Fire safety rules follow the National Building Code (NBC) 2005; the type and number of fire safety items depend on the industry's size and risk, with stricter rules for high-risk units.

(Session 1) The application is made online on the single window portal, so no one needs to visit a government office to submit it; the department then checks details and inspects the premises before occupation/operations begin.
(Session 1) No major delay was reported; inspection is generally done within about 7 working days of submission, though this can differ by case.
(Session 1) Give the Fire NOC a validity of 3 to 5 years, continuing yearly inspections where needed, and accept modular fire extinguishers as a regular option wherever sprinklers cannot be used.
(Session 1) The government fee depends on building area/size and is paid online; no separate inspection fee was mentioned.
(Session 2, Nellore) Lack of training on fire requirements was the main initial pain point; some requirements and newer fire systems are not widely understood.

(Session 2) Each block of the establishment (east, west, north, south) is treated as a separate entity; for each block the applicant must show a diagram, extinguisher counts/kinds, specifications and pictures, which participants found difficult.

(Session 2) Renewal gap: participants applied 15–20 days before expiry, the officer visited 10–15 days later, and the certificate was issued after the old one had expired, creating audit and export-compliance risk; the officer being busy with other renewals delays inspection.

(Session 2) Renewal rule requires applying 60 days before expiry; the NOC is issued for 3 years (challan showed only 3 years); fee depends on number of years (1/3/5), number of blocks and type of operation, with inspection charges separate.

(Session 2) Inspection follows about 10–15 days after submission; after inspection the department lists observations, the applicant corrects them, and a second inspection is held before the NOC is issued; remarks are routed onward (to head office) before approval.

(Session 2) Inspection scheduling (10–15 days), remarks routed onward (2–3 days), and applying only 15–20 days before expiry against a 60-day window together contributed to delay in the renewal cases discussed.

(Session 2) Issue the renewal certificate from the date of expiry itself (no break in the cycle) where delay is on the department side, and extend NOC validity from 3 to 5 years where operations are standard and unchanged.
(Session 2) Fire department to run training programmes every 6 months or at short intervals.

(Session 2) Participants were comfortable with the fire department overall, describing the process flow as good with no bottleneck at the application stage; pre-construction plan-stage guidance was cited positively, as was online payment helping avoid corruption.

(Session 2) Inspection is done only by the fire department, not by a third party; a yearly inspection takes place irrespective of renewal; purchase from state-empanelled vendors is not compulsory and the department is open to updated technology.

findings.text: Parts of the GST registration application are tricky; mistakes are easy to make and take a lot of time to rectify, so many applicants rely on a CA.
The GST portal is slow and its refresh time is high; during return filing the page refreshes and the information is lost, so filing has to be repeated several times.

Input tax credit set-off is applied automatically; when taken from CGST it also affects the SGST side (split half and half), causing problems for the customer filing the return, with no option to choose the component.
Quarterly filers still have monthly tax adjustment: only one month is settled in the filing and the balance for the other two months has to be filed again.

Companies face many legal issues in registration and need professional guidance; misleading information circulates on social media, with no reliable simple guidance for people who are not digitally literate.
Nobody in the group could give an approximate timeframe for GST refunds after filing.
Registration requires a lease deed or rent agreement for the premises; for partnerships, the partnership deed and trade licence are also asked for.
Monthly or quarterly filing is optional only up to a turnover of about ₹1.5 crore; above that, monthly filing is mandatory (stated by the moderator and confirmed in discussion).
The whole application is online: documents are scanned and uploaded as PDFs; participants found the portal easy to understand and said registration is much smoother than in 2017.
Registration is issued in about 7 days, provided all documents are uploaded correctly.
Mistakes in the registration application take long to correct, and the 7-day registration timeline holds only if all documents are uploaded correctly.
Give entrepreneurs an option to choose which tax component (CGST/SGST/IGST) the set-off is taken from at the time of filing.
Provide short videos on how to register, file and renew rather than relying on documents.
Improve portal speed and fix the refresh problem that wipes entered information.
For quarterly filers, allow tax adjustment and filing for all 3 months together, and allow adjusting a balance left in one tax component against another.
Align rate or slab changes with the start of the financial year, since business software has to be updated.

Several participants said they had no pain point; many file through a CA or accountant because they are used to it and prefer to outsource rather than spend time, although quarterly returns can be filed without an intermediary.
Social media makes people aware of GST but also spreads viral claims that cannot be trusted.

findings.text: Documentation requirements were not sufficiently clear for applicants, creating dependence on physical assistance and office visits.
Limited clarity was reported regarding vacant plots, the specific site allotted, usable area, irregular land shape and space that may need to be retained for green areas.
After allotment, substantial time, effort and expenditure may be required for land filling and making the site ready for construction.
The helpdesk number on the single-desk portal was reported to remain continuously busy, limiting its usefulness for applicants seeking assistance.

Requirements and approvals may vary according to the proposed line of activity, land size, location and site-specific conditions; clearer upfront indication of applicability was identified as necessary.
The availability and timing of subsidies were not clear; earlier land-allotment/transformer-related subsidies were also reported as no longer available.
Applicants may incur interest on the outstanding land amount after allotment, adding to the financial burden of establishing the unit.

Although the process is supported through an online portal, lack of clarity on the website resulted in applicants visiting offices physically, in some cases returning when the concerned person was unavailable.
Application status tracking was reported as unavailable or insufficient, making it difficult to know the current position of an application.
In some cases, applicants may discover only after allotment that the usable portion of the site is smaller than expected or subject to additional conditions, requiring further action.
Support through the District Industries Centre (DIC) was described as useful for applicants who require assistance in understanding or completing the process.
No specific instance of significant duplication or repeated submission of the same documents was identified.
Delays were associated with land filling and preparation of the allotted plot, obtaining required utilities (including groundwater connection), and lack of adequate road access for larger industries.
Where an unsuitable or incorrectly understood site is identified after allotment, returning the land and processing it again through the system can consume additional time.
Provide a ready reckoner, template or pamphlet clearly listing documents applicants need to keep ready, and provide activity-specific guidance through FAQs and guidance videos.
Provide advance information on vacant sites, the specific site likely to be allotted, usable area, green-space requirements, approach roads and other site conditions before application/allotment.
Introduce reliable application-status tracking, and improve the single-desk portal and helpdesk accessibility and responsiveness.
Clearly communicate subsidy eligibility, expected timelines and the applicable quantum of subsidy.

One experience indicated that after receiving appropriate guidance, the process became easier and approvals were obtained quickly; however interest on outstanding land amounts, utility-related expenditure and other establishment costs can add to the financial pressure on businesses, particularly MSMEs.

findings.text: There are no clear-cut fire safety guidelines; requirements (pumps, hydrants, extinguishers, spacing) change from officer to officer, and applicants depend on consultants to work out what applies. In one case a district officer insisted on plunger pumps costing almost ₹1 crore; nobody has asked for them since he left.
Inspectors and the APPCB sometimes ask for equipment beyond the minimum standard, such as an RO plant or extra STP/ETP capacity, depending on the individual inspector.

Approvals that fall to the district administration, such as the storage and usage NOC for naphtha, diesel or sulphur after PESO approval, are not part of the single window portal; participants say they have asked repeatedly for it to be added — 'the site exists but we have to open every door.'

For a phased expansion at the same location (second and third phases), the portal does not accept IEM Part B, saying it is already issued; this was resolved only through an alternate arrangement after a lot of back-and-forth between departments.

The fire occupancy certificate was cut from 5 years to 1 year for the red category (rule changed at the end of 2023); participants said no intimation of the change was received, and other categories were given 2-3 years. Without the fire certificate, no other department gives approval.

AP still insists on 33% green belt (22% by the company and 11% by APIIC), although MoEF&CC and CPCB now allow 15% for the red category; participants say this blocks land needed for development and expansion.
Fire requirements are now inspected by the local DFO on the basis of central guidelines, whereas earlier companies gave an undertaking with occasional random inspections.

Three certificates sit under 'occupancy': the local authority's building OC, the fire OC, and the structural certificate already taken under the factory license; states treat these differently. The Date of Commercial Production (DCP), issued by DIC only after OC, factory license and CFO are verified, is the starting point for loans, benefits and incentives.
The sequence described is: construction, then CFE, then CFO (consent to operate), then trial production, then DCP and the occupancy certificates.

A minor improvement need not be reported; a major change must be reported to the Industries Department and the CFE amended, with additional equipment going to Factories, a process modification to APPCB, product changes (pharma) to Drug Control, and an additional building to the planning authority, after which the OC comes up again.

On renewal, red-category units are sent again to 7–9 departments, including the revenue department, which checks for a burial ground, school or hospital inside the plant — already cleared when the initial NOC was granted.

The stated service level is a 21-day turnaround (some permissions in 7 days); a department representative said about 99% of approvals are within SLA, with delays mainly in petroleum-product NOCs, which need 7 departments.

Participants reported the district-administration NOC taking more than 2 months, and about 6 months in some cases; files are referred to departments unconnected with the plant, which inspect in their own time.
Bring the district-administration approvals online into the single window, and avoid re-inspection by 7 departments at renewal once the initial NOC is issued, unless the plant is modified.
Restore longer validity for the fire OC (2 years at least, ideally 5), with periodic audits or checks for companies that do not comply.
Adopt the CPCB/MoEF 15% green belt norm in AP, and allow the green belt to be developed on land outside the plant within a radius.

Publish clear, uniform fire guidelines and communicate rule changes effectively, with online FAQs and guidelines by industry size and profile; make IEM Part B work for phased expansion at the same location.
The department representative pointed to FAQs, Government Orders and the Commissionerate of Industries EoDB wing online, plus a TCS-run support team available 24 hours.
